input.question: How/Why did organisms go from single cell division to requiring a separate partner to reproduce?
input.ground_truth: I've always tied it to the invention of meiosis. Mitosis divides cells, but meiosis make half-cell kits, that can then combine in rapidly expanding numbers of ways. I see it as several billion years of mitosis and then meiosis gets discovered and boom: Cambrian Explosion.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How/Why did organisms go from single cell division to requiring a separate partner to reproduce?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have one tiny Lego block. That’s like a single cell. At first, that one block can make a copy of itself and you get two blocks. That’s how single cells can divide and make more of themselves.

But as time went on, some of these tiny blocks started working together to make bigger and more complicated things, like a big Lego castle. These bigger things (which are now living things made of many cells) are more complicated, and sometimes one block by itself isn’t enough to make a new castle.

So, to make a new, healthy castle (or a new living thing), two different Lego builders (or cells) work together. They each bring something special, and when they work together, they can build something even better and healthier. That’s why some living things need a partner to make new babies—they work together to make something amazing that one alone can’t do.

So, as living things got bigger and fancier, they needed a helper to make new ones!
